To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

calcium‐pyroantimonate precipitation is an excellent technique for visualizing Ca2+ in the microvilli of oocyte membranes in Drosophila, and that electron energy‐loss and electron spectroscopic imaging can be used to determine the elemental composition of such precipitates.

calcium precipitates are found in the oolemma microvilli of mid‐ and late stage vitellogenic Drosophila follicles, and that the precipitates are composed of calcium, oxygen and antimony, but not nitrogen.

the microvilli of mid‐ to late vitellogenis follicles are lined with precipitates of Ca2+‐antimonate and that these precipitates contain antimony, calcium and oxygen, as demonstrated by electron spectroscopic and electron energy‐‐loss spectroscopy.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the application of electron spectroscopic imaging to the study of the distribution and chemical composition of precipitates formed by the reaction of calcium ions with antimonate in the microvillar membrane of the follicular epithelium in vitellogeneic follicles of D. melanogaster.
the localization of calcium in Drosophila vitellogenic oocytes.
the application of ESI and EELS for the analysis of the elemental composition of biological specimens.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the precipitates formed by the reaction with pyroantimonates contain Ca2+, oxygen and antimony.
the microvilli of oolemma in Drosophila follicles are lined with calcium‐antimonate precipitated from a medium rich in calcium and antimony.
the precipitates contain Ca2+, antimonate and oxygen and that they do not contain nitrogen.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the precipitates formed in the mid‐ and late‐vitellogenic follicle are composed of calcium and antimony, and that they are probably formed from the yolk protein precursor, the vitellogenin.
ESI and EELS are powerful tools in the study of cellular structures and their elemental composition.
ESI is a powerful tool in elemental mapping and EELS is a useful tool in elemental analysis of specific structures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of potassium antimonate as a Ca2+-precipitating reagent is suitable for electron microscopic analysis of the Ca2+-binding sites in Drosophila vitellogenic oocytes.
the elemental analysis can be performed without the need to remove the precipitates from the tissue.

we have shown that the use of electron spectroscopic imaging and electron energy‐lose spectroscopy in conjunction with electron microscopy allows for the elemental composition of reaction products to be analysed in a high spatial resolution.
